faqs.q: How do I know if the droppings in my New Brunswick basement are from rats?
faqs.a: Rat droppings are capsule-shaped and about half an inch long — much larger than mouse droppings — and they concentrate along walls, near food storage, and beside the grease-dark rub marks rats leave on the routes they run nightly. In the rental blocks the basement signs gather where the old oil tank and the sewer lateral share a wall, and the turnover cleaning crews are usually the first to report them. A rat job here is three parts: trapping out the animals present, sealing the entries (a rat needs only a half-inch gap), and cutting the food and harborage that drew them. Any baiting, where it is used at all, follows New Jersey's pesticide rules.

faqs.q: Do you charge to inspect a New Brunswick attic?
faqs.a: The inspection is the working visit: roofline, attic, and foundation get checked, entries get photographed, and you receive a written quote for the full job. New Brunswick inspections note the occupancy calendar, because an entry sealed during a vacant week, with the whole unit accessible, is a cheaper and better job than the same work around tenants. That sequence — inspect first, quote in writing, then remove and seal — is how every job here runs, so there are no surprise line items after the animals are already out.

New Brunswick.wildlife_intro:
New Brunswick layers a college city over an old river port: Rutgers blocks and student rentals near College Avenue, older neighborhoods of twins and singles across town, and the Raritan River closing the north side. Rats lead the call log, working the restaurant corridors, the older sewer laterals, and the basements of the rental stock. Raccoons den in the porch roofs and chimneys of the older streets, squirrels take the eaves near the parks and campuses, and starlings and sparrows nest in the vents above the commercial strips. Turnover is constant, and vacant weeks are when animals sign their leases.

Attached housing changes the math. In a rowhouse or twin, one animal in a shared attic or party-wall void is every neighbor's problem, and sealing a single unit while the adjoining roofline stays open just moves the tenant sideways. We inspect the whole run of connected rooflines where access allows, coordinate timing with neighbors when entries cross property lines, and seal the full set of openings under one plan. Older masonry party walls hide voids that let squirrels travel between houses unseen — finding those routes is most of the job in attached stock. New Brunswick's twins and triples share roofs and voids, so entries are mapped across the connected buildings and the sealing is scheduled so no animal is pushed from one unit into the next.

faqs.q: Why do I hear running in my Edison ceiling every morning?
faqs.a: Daytime running, especially at dawn and mid-afternoon, points to gray squirrels — they commute. In Oak Tree's wooded streets the morning running starts where the canopy touches the gable, and the same corner detail fails on house after house built in the same year. A squirrel entry is usually a gnawed widening at a gable vent, dormer cheek, or eave return, and the repair has to replace the chewed wood and back it with metal, or the next squirrel reopens it in days. One-way doors let the animals leave on their own schedule; then the opening is closed for good.

faqs.q: A groundhog is burrowing under my Edison foundation — how bad is that?
faqs.a: Worse than it looks. A groundhog burrow system runs many feet with several chambers, and soil removed from under a slab or footing leaves voids that crack concrete and channel water against the foundation. Edison's park-edge lots give groundhogs a wooded bank to den in and a garden to commute to, and the burrow in the bank is where the trapping plan starts, not the hole at the deck. We trap at the active entrances, then backfill and screen the site so the next groundhog inherits a closed burrow. Groundhogs are on New Jersey's rabies-vector list — one more reason not to corner one yourself.

Edison.wildlife_intro:
Edison is Middlesex County in miniature, a huge township of distinct sections: Clara Barton's older streets, Menlo Park, Oak Tree's wooded lots, and the postwar subdivisions of North and South Edison, all stitched together by Routes 1, 27, and 287. Squirrels and raccoons are the township's daily bread, entering the colonials and split-levels at soffits and gable vents under a heavy canopy. Groundhogs work the bigger lots and the Roosevelt Park edges, rats appear around the older commercial corridors, and bats take the quieter attics near the Raritan and the park woods.

Most entries are not holes animals made — they are building failures animals found. Fascia boards rot behind gutters, soffit panels sag at the seams, and a gray squirrel needs only a small gap and one afternoon to widen it. Repairs here mean replacing the rotted wood, not just covering it, then backing vents and eave returns with metal that teeth cannot work through. Paint-matched covers keep the fix invisible from the street. Gutters clogged with leaf litter matter too: standing water softens the very boards that are supposed to keep animals out. Edison's subdivisions were built in waves with the same details repeated street after street, so a soffit failure here is treated as a pattern, and the whole run is checked and priced as a run.

faqs.q: There is heavy thumping in my Woodbridge Township attic at night — is it a raccoon?
faqs.a: Heavy, deliberate thumping after dark is the classic raccoon signature; squirrels sound lighter and keep daytime hours. In Colonia's postwar colonials the thumping usually enters at the junction of the garage roof and the house wall, a detail the whole subdivision shares. We locate the entry — often a pushed-up soffit or a vent the animal has peeled back — check for a litter before anything moves, and get the family out together. Because raccoons sit on New Jersey's rabies-vector list, droppings and latrine areas in the attic get treated as contaminated material, not swept aside.

faqs.q: We keep catching rats around our Woodbridge Township home — why do they come back?
faqs.a: Because the route and the restaurant are still open. Norway rats commute along fence lines, ivy, and utility runs, and they stay where trash, pet food, or a bird feeder feeds them every single night. Near Port Reading and the older corridors the rat runs follow the rail and fence lines into the residential blocks, and the properties that stay clear are the ones with mortared entries and nothing edible stored low. We map the runs, seal the building entries in metal and mortar — rats gnaw through foam and wood — and go over the sanitation changes that make the property stop paying out. Trapping alone, without those two halves, is a subscription, not a solution.

Woodbridge Township.wildlife_intro:
Woodbridge is a township of villages: Woodbridge proper with its older Main Street homes, Avenel and Colonia's postwar streets, Iselin's subdivisions, Fords, and industrial Port Reading on the Arthur Kill. The water and the industry shape the calls. Rats hold the industrial edges and the older corridors, raccoons work every village's chimneys and the creek corridors, squirrels fill the Colonia and Avenel attics, and groundhogs dig along the rail lines and the Woodbridge River banks. Each village has its own housing era and its own version of the same animals.

Food decides where animals settle. Bird feeders spill seed that feeds rats at night, pet dishes sit out on porches, trash waits in cans a raccoon can open in seconds, and fallen fruit ferments under backyard trees. Removal without changing that menu is a short truce. We go over the property's food map with the homeowner — secured cans, feeders on baffled poles set away from the house, fruit picked up, grills cleaned — because the houses that stay quiet are the ones that stop advertising. The animal work and the housekeeping have to happen together. Woodbridge's corridor jobs pair the sealing with the back-lot food audit, because the blocks behind the strips will keep restocking a property that leaves the menu out.

faqs.q: Why can't I get an exact wildlife quote for my Piscataway Township home over the phone?
faqs.a: Because the same scratching sound can mean a short fix or a colony that has been overhead for two seasons — nobody honest can price it from a description. A Possumtown farmhouse with raccoons in a stone chimney and a new subdivision home with starlings in a plastic vent are both Piscataway inspections in the same week, and the written quotes reflect how different those jobs are. After the inspection you hold a written figure covering removal, entry sealing, and cleanup, and the work does not begin until you approve it.

faqs.q: Once the animals are out of my Piscataway Township home, how do I keep them out?
faqs.a: Walk the house the way an animal does: roofline first, then vents, then ground level. Chimney cap, metal-backed vent covers, limbs cut back off the roof, trash in lidded cans, and no pet food or open seed stored in the garage. River-side Piscataway homes get the fall list with the water in mind: the entries on the park-facing side of the house are the ones the commuting animals test first. We leave you the entry map from your own job — which gaps were sealed and which aging spots to watch — because the houses that stay quiet are checked each fall, not just fixed once.

Piscataway Township.wildlife_intro:
Piscataway spreads along the Raritan across from New Brunswick: older neighborhoods like Possumtown and New Market, postwar subdivisions, Rutgers' Busch and Livingston campuses at its edges, and Johnson Park's riverfront green. The river and the park woods keep the township stocked. Raccoons den in the chimneys of the older sections, squirrels work the subdivision canopy, groundhogs dig the park-edge and field-edge lots, and bats take attics near the river. The housing is old enough in places for a century of gaps and new enough elsewhere for the modern plastic-vent failures.

Newer houses are not exempt — they just fail differently. Vinyl soffits flex and pop at the corners, roof-to-wall joints on additions open as materials settle, and bathroom vents often end in cheap plastic covers that starlings and squirrels push through in a season. Builders leave gaps around garage door corners and utility lines that rats and mice find within the first year. The work on a newer home is detail work: metal where plastic failed, backer rod and sealant at settling joints, and screens behind every vent cover rather than trust in the cover alone. Piscataway inspections run both eras' checklists, the pre-war gap list in Possumtown and New Market, and the vent-and-vinyl list in the newer subdivisions, sometimes on the same street.

faqs.q: There is a dead-animal smell in my Perth Amboy house but I can't find anything — can you?
faqs.a: Yes — locating it is a method, not a guess. Smell intensity, fly activity, and the floor plan narrow it to a wall void, a crawlspace corner, or a stretch of ductwork, and we open the smallest section that lets us remove the carcass. In Perth Amboy's older twins the smell usually settles in a first-floor wall on the bay side, and the fly activity at one window generally marks the void before any cutting is discussed. The spot then gets disinfected and deodorized, and we check how the animal got in, because a carcass in a wall usually means an entry that is still open. Carcasses of rabies-vector species are handled with gloves and bagged, never bare-handed.

faqs.q: Birds nest in my Perth Amboy bathroom vent every spring — what can be done?
faqs.a: Usually European starlings or house sparrows, the two species New Jersey's Game Code lets us deal with directly when they damage property. The nest comes out, the vent gets cleaned of the mites and debris nests carry, and a proper vent cover with a screen behind it ends the annual tenancy. Downtown's older buildings give starlings a vent or a sign cabinet on nearly every facade, and the residential units above the shops inherit the nesting season whether they want it or not. Native birds are a different matter — a chimney swift or swallow nest means timing and deterrence work only, and we will tell you honestly which bird you have before anything is touched.

Perth Amboy.wildlife_intro:
Perth Amboy is a small, dense port city on Raritan Bay: a historic waterfront of older homes around State Street, grid streets of twins and small apartment buildings, and industry along the Arthur Kill and the bay. Rats are the city's first wildlife fact, working the waterfront, the older sewers, and the blocks behind the food corridors. Raccoons den in the chimneys and porch roofs of the older housing, starlings and sparrows occupy the signs and vents downtown, and opossums commute from the marshy edges into the crawlspaces. The bay keeps the whole city within a short walk of habitat.

Crawlspaces collect problems quietly. A vent screen rusts through, a pipe penetration was never sealed, and within a season the space underneath the house holds opossums, skunks, or a raccoon latrine — along with the odor that rides the ductwork upstairs. The fix starts with a light and a full circuit underneath: every vent screened in metal, gaps around plumbing and wiring sealed, and any carcass or waste taken out. Where moisture is part of the draw, we say so plainly, because a damp crawlspace keeps attracting animals no matter how well it is screened. Perth Amboy's crawlspaces sit close to bay water, and the screening specification here assumes damp, salt air and checks the sill for the rot that comes with both.

faqs.q: Can you get a raccoon family out of a Old Bridge Township chimney?
faqs.a: Yes — spring raccoon mothers choose uncapped chimneys across Middlesex County. Our crew checks whether pups are present before anything moves, removes the family together whenever we can, and fits a proper chimney cap so the same chimney is not a den again next spring.

In fall and winter, squirrels and rodents push into warm attics and wall voids in Old Bridge Township; spring brings denning raccoons and groundhog and skunk activity in yards, and summer is bat and mole season. Most Old Bridge Township jobs start with a full roofline and foundation inspection, then removal and sealing of every entry we find, because closing only the obvious hole rarely holds.

faqs.q: Moles are tearing up my East Brunswick yard — how are they handled?
faqs.a: By trapping the active runs, not by poison peanuts or vibrating stakes, which mostly rearrange the damage. Surface ridges are feeding tunnels; the deep runs along edges and foundations are the travel lanes where traps belong. East Brunswick's irrigated lawns over sandy soil are mole motorways, and the runs here often connect three yards before they surface as the mounds that get reported. Eastern moles work most New Jersey lawns, and the star-nosed mole turns up in wetter ground. Expect a few visits spaced out — mole work is verified by fresh ridging stopping, not by a single day's catch.

faqs.q: Are squirrels in a East Brunswick attic actually a fire risk?
faqs.a: They can be. Squirrels gnaw constantly to wear their teeth, and wiring, PVC, and stored paper are all fair game; chewed conductors in a hot attic are a genuine hazard, not a sales line. The 1970s attics here combine squirrel traffic with aging wiring, and chewed runs get photographed as a standard part of the sealing visit. Once the squirrels are out and the entries are meshed, we flag any chewed wiring we saw so an electrician can judge it — that check is part of why a squirrel job should never end at just closing the hole.

East Brunswick.wildlife_intro:
East Brunswick is a Route 18 suburb that grew in layers: older capes and ranches from the first postwar wave, big 1970s subdivisions, and newer colonials out toward Milltown and South River. Lawrence Brook and Farrington Lake thread the township with green corridors. Squirrels and raccoons work the mature-canopy subdivisions, groundhogs dig the brook-side and field-edge lots, moles ridge the big watered lawns, and bats take the attics near the lake and the woods. The housing stock's age means original soffits and vents are failing across whole neighborhoods at once.

The quiet months are the test. Anyone can empty an attic; keeping it empty through the next breeding season is the work. We leave each house with its entries mapped — what was sealed, with what material, and what to watch — and we flag the two or three weak points most likely to fail next, whether that is aging flashing, a settling addition, or a tree that will reach the roof in two more summers. Homeowners who walk that list each fall, the way they service a furnace, rarely meet us twice for the same animal. East Brunswick's subdivisions age in cohorts, and when one house on a street reports a soffit entry, the inspection here treats the neighbors' identical details as a warning worth mentioning.
